questions.q: Monopolar radiofrequency (RF) devices (e.g., Thermage) produce skin tightening via which mechanism?
opts: Selective photothermolysis of dermal collagen fibres matching thermal relaxation time
Resistive (ohmic) heating of dermal tissue causing immediate collagen contraction and delayed neocollagenesis
Ultrasound cavitation disrupting fibroblast membranes to stimulate collagen synthesis
Photochemical crosslinking of collagen fibres by near-infrared photons
questions.exp: RF current passes through tissue, generating heat via electrical resistance (ohmic heating) independent of chromophores. Temperatures of 65–75°C cause immediate collagen fibre contraction (triple-helix denaturation), followed over 3–6 months by neocollagenesis from thermally activated fibroblasts. RF penetration depth is inversely proportional to frequency — lower frequencies penetrate more deeply.

questions.q: High-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU, Ultherapy) achieves tissue lifting by creating discrete thermal coagulation zones (TCZs). At what depths do standard transducers target the dermis and SMAS respectively?
opts: 0.5 mm (epidermis) and 1.5 mm (superficial dermis)
1.5 mm (dermis), 3.0 mm (deep dermis), and 4.5 mm (SMAS/superficial fascia)
3.0 mm (dermis) and 8.0 mm (deep fat/SMAS)
2.0 mm (papillary dermis) and 6.0 mm (subcutaneous fat)
questions.exp: HIFU focuses acoustic energy to discrete points generating 60–70°C in TCZs at 1.5 mm (superficial dermis), 3.0 mm (deep dermis), and 4.5 mm (SMAS layer) without affecting overlying or intervening tissue. Immediate SMAS contraction plus 3–6 month collagen remodelling produces tissue lifting. Real-time ultrasound imaging confirms transducer coupling and target depth.

questions.q: Cryolipolysis (CoolSculpting) selectively destroys subcutaneous adipocytes at temperatures of −5°C to +5°C while sparing the overlying dermis. The basis for this selectivity is:
opts: Adipocyte membranes are thinner than keratinocyte membranes, rupturing at lower temperatures
High lipid content of adipocytes allows fatty acid crystallisation at temperatures tolerated by the water-rich dermis and epidermis, triggering selective cold-induced apoptosis
Adipocytes express cold-sensitive TRP channels (TRPM8) that mediate calcium influx causing membrane lysis
Subcutaneous fat has lower thermal conductivity, retaining cold longer than dermis and causing preferential ice crystal formation
questions.exp: Adipocyte selectivity is based on differential cold sensitivity: high lipid content allows fatty acid crystallisation at −5°C to +5°C, initiating apoptosis. Overlying dermis and epidermis contain predominantly water (higher freezing point resistance) and survive these temperatures. The controlled apoptotic process — not necrosis — triggers an inflammatory response with macrophage phagocytosis of lipid debris over 1–3 months, reducing fat layer thickness by 20–25%.

questions.q: ATX-101 (deoxycholic acid 1%, Kybella) reduces submental fat volume by:
opts: Activating β₃-adrenergic receptors in adipocytes to stimulate cyclic-AMP-mediated lipolysis
Detergent-mediated lysis of adipocyte plasma membranes, causing cytolysis and local inflammatory fibrosis
Blocking PPARγ nuclear receptor to inhibit preadipocyte differentiation
Inhibiting hormone-sensitive lipase via cAMP suppression, trapping triglycerides within adipocytes until apoptosis occurs
questions.exp: Deoxycholic acid is a bile acid detergent that disrupts phospholipid bilayers of adipocyte membranes (non-selectively), causing cytolysis → inflammatory response → fibrosis and fat volume reduction. Surrounding non-adipose tissues are also susceptible — marginal mandibular nerve injury (temporary or permanent smile asymmetry) is the most serious complication. Maximum dose per session: 10 mL (100 mg).

questions.q: IPL (Intense Pulsed Light) devices differ fundamentally from lasers for hair removal. Which property makes IPL less selective than a single-wavelength laser?
opts: IPL pulses are shorter than laser pulses, reducing thermal damage to target chromophores

IPL uses non-coherent, broad-spectrum polychromatic light (515–1200 nm), with cutoff filters selecting a wavelength range — simultaneously targeting multiple chromophores with lower selectivity per chromophore
IPL penetrates more superficially than Nd:YAG laser due to epidermal scatter of the broad spectrum
IPL cannot be used on FST I–II skin as melanin absorption causes guaranteed burns
questions.exp: Lasers are monochromatic, coherent, and collimated — targeting one chromophore with maximum selectivity. IPL emits broad-spectrum non-coherent light filtered by cutoff filters (e.g., 695 nm filter for hair in FST I–III). Multiple chromophores (melanin + oxyhemoglobin) absorb simultaneously, reducing selectivity. In darker skin types (FST IV–VI), epidermal melanin competes with follicular melanin absorption, increasing burn risk — Nd:YAG 1064 nm is safer.

questions.q: For diode 810 nm laser hair removal, which parameter is MOST critical to selectively destroy the follicle (bulge + dermal papilla) while sparing the epidermis?
opts: Wavelength — must be changed to 755 nm for all hair types for optimal melanin absorption
Spot size — larger spots increase fluence uniformity and minimise edge scatter
Pulse duration — must match the thermal relaxation time (TRT) of the entire follicular unit (40–100 ms for terminal hair), not just individual melanin granules
Repetition rate — burst mode at 10 Hz creates cumulative sub-threshold heating without individual pulse tissue injury
questions.exp: Selective photothermolysis for hair removal requires pulse duration matching the TRT of the entire follicular structure (40–100 ms for a terminal follicle — far longer than the TRT of melanin granules in microseconds). Pulses this long selectively heat the whole follicular unit including the germ cells (bulge + papilla) through heat diffusion from follicular melanin, while cryogen spray or contact cooling protects the overlying epidermis. Coarser hair has a longer TRT and requires longer pulses.

questions.q: Standard botulinum toxin injection for glabellar frown lines targets which muscles?
opts: Frontalis, orbicularis oculi, and zygomaticus major
Corrugator supercilii, procerus, and depressor supercilii (±medial orbicularis oculi)
Frontalis and levator palpebrae superioris
Nasalis and procerus only
questions.exp: The glabellar complex producing '11 lines' comprises: corrugator supercilii (medial brow depression/adduction → oblique lines), procerus (nasal root depression → horizontal lines), and depressor supercilii with medial orbicularis oculi fibres (medial brow depression). FDA-approved onabotulinumtoxinA dose: 20 U across 5 injection points. Injecting frontalis here risks brow ptosis.

questions.q: A patient develops unilateral upper eyelid ptosis 10 days after forehead botulinum toxin injection. The mechanism and management are:
opts: Direct levator palpebrae injection — irreversible; wait 3–4 months for complete toxin wear-off
Toxin diffusion through the orbital septum from a suprabrow injection to the levator palpebrae superioris; managed with apraclonidine 0.5% eye drops (α₂-agonist stimulating Müller's muscle)
Allergic periorbital oedema causing mechanical ptosis — treat with oral antihistamines
Frontalis paralysis causing brow ptosis — lift the brow manually to confirm eyelid is unaffected
questions.exp: Lid ptosis post-forehead botox results from toxin diffusion (not direct injection) through the orbital septum when injection sites are too close to the orbital rim (<1 cm). Apraclonidine 0.5% eye drops (alpha-agonist) stimulate Müller's muscle (a sympathetically innervated accessory lid elevator), partially lifting the lid by 1–2 mm within 10 minutes — used until toxin effect wanes (~6–8 weeks). Prevention: inject ≥1 cm above orbital rim, avoid post-injection massage.

questions.q: Calcium hydroxylapatite (CaHA, Radiesse) differs critically from HA fillers because:
opts: It is reversible with hyaluronidase injection, making vascular occlusion manageable
CaHA microspheres provide immediate volume AND serve as a scaffold for autologous collagen deposition (biostimulation) over 12–18 months, with NO available reversal agent
CaHA is contraindicated in the lips due to risk of nodule formation but approved for periorbital use
CaHA has no risk of the Tyndall effect since it is not optically transparent like HA
questions.exp: CaHA (Radiesse) provides dual action: immediate volume from gel carrier + long-term biostimulation as CaHA microspheres (25–45 μm) scaffold fibroblast attachment → type I collagen synthesis. Results last 12–18 months. Critically, there is NO reversal agent — unlike HA fillers (reversed with hyaluronidase). Vascular occlusion with CaHA is a medical emergency requiring warm compresses, nitropaste, aspirin, and possibly hyperbaric oxygen.

questions.q: Poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA, Sculptra) is classified as a 'biostimulatory' filler. The correct mechanism and treatment interval are:
opts: PLLA particles act as osmotic agents, drawing tissue fluid to create immediate and sustained volume
PLLA microparticles trigger controlled foreign body response → fibroblast activation → type I collagen neosynthesis as particles degrade over 6–12 months; requires 2–3 sessions spaced 4–6 weeks apart
PLLA cross-links with endogenous HA to create a hybrid scaffold with immediate and long-term volume
PLLA is phagocytosed by adipocytes, stimulating lipogenesis and soft tissue volume in treated areas
questions.exp: PLLA microparticles (2–50 μm) are phagocytosed by macrophages, triggering a controlled foreign body granulomatous response that activates fibroblasts to deposit new collagen. As PLLA hydrolyses to lactic acid → CO₂ + H₂O over 6–12 months, the neo-collagen scaffold maintains volume for 2+ years. Results are gradual (not immediate). Protocol: 2–3 sessions 4–6 weeks apart; avoid over-injection which risks nodule formation.

questions.q: Azelaic acid's depigmenting mechanism is distinct from kojic acid. It works by:
opts: Chelating copper from the tyrosinase active site (same mechanism as kojic acid)
Competitive inhibition of tyrosinase with selective cytotoxic and antiproliferative effects on hyperactive (melasma/PIH) melanocytes, sparing normally functioning melanocytes
Blocking PAR-2 receptors to prevent melanosome transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes
Photochemical destruction of melanin via singlet oxygen generation under UV exposure
questions.exp: Azelaic acid competitively inhibits tyrosinase but uniquely exerts selective antiproliferative and mildly cytotoxic effects on hyperactive melanocytes (as in melasma and PIH) while sparing normally functioning melanocytes — making it safer for long-term use than hydroquinone. Additional mechanisms: normalises follicular keratinisation (comedolytic), inhibits Cutibacterium acnes (bacteriostatic), and inhibits 5α-reductase (anti-androgenic).

questions.q: Niacinamide (vitamin B₃, 4–5%) reduces skin pigmentation by a mechanism DIFFERENT from tyrosinase inhibitors. It acts by:
opts: Inhibiting DOPA oxidase at the rate-limiting step of melanin biosynthesis
Inhibiting protease-activated receptor 2 (PAR-2)-mediated melanosome transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes
Increasing epidermal cell turnover, accelerating loss of pigmented keratinocytes
Blocking melanocortin-1 receptor (MC1R) to reduce α-MSH-driven melanogenesis
questions.exp: Niacinamide inhibits the transfer of melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes by interfering with PAR-2 (protease-activated receptor 2) signalling — the mechanism by which keratinocytes phagocytose melanosomes. It does NOT inhibit tyrosinase. Clinical studies show 4% niacinamide matches 4% hydroquinone in reducing facial pigmentation with better tolerability. Additional benefits: barrier enhancement, anti-inflammatory, sebostatic.

questions.q: Spironolactone is used off-label for female pattern hair loss (FPHL). Its primary mechanism is:
opts: Inhibition of 5α-reductase type 2, reducing DHT conversion in dermal papilla cells
Competitive antagonism of androgen receptors (AR) in hair follicle dermal papilla, preventing DHT binding and follicular miniaturisation signalling
Inhibition of adrenal androgen synthesis (DHEA, androstenedione) via CYP17A1 blockade
Potassium channel opening in dermal papilla cells, mimicking minoxidil's mechanism
questions.exp: Spironolactone primarily blocks androgen receptors (AR) in target tissues including hair follicle dermal papilla cells, preventing DHT binding and downstream miniaturisation. It also mildly reduces adrenal androgen synthesis. Standard dose: 100–200 mg/day for FPHL. Key contraindications: pregnancy (teratogenic feminisation of male fetus — must use contraception), hyperkalaemia, renal impairment. Monitor serum potassium and blood pressure.

questions.q: For intralesional corticosteroid injection in alopecia areata (AA), the optimal technique is:
opts: Triamcinolone acetonide 40 mg/mL injected deep subcutaneously for a long-lasting depot effect
Triamcinolone acetonide 5–10 mg/mL injected intradermally (0.1 mL per site, 1 cm intervals) targeting perifollicular dermal inflammation
Betamethasone valerate 0.1% applied topically under polyethylene occlusion for 24 hours
Hydrocortisone 20 mg/mL intralesionally to avoid dermal atrophy while retaining anti-inflammatory efficacy
questions.exp: Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide (ILT) 5–10 mg/mL injected intradermally at 0.1 mL per site, 1 cm apart is first-line for patchy AA. Intradermal (not subcutaneous) placement targets perifollicular inflammatory infiltrate directly. Higher concentrations (40 mg/mL) or subcutaneous injection cause fat atrophy and telangiectasia. Maximum dose per session: ~20 mg. Repeated every 4–6 weeks. Eyebrow/eyelash AA: use lower concentration (2.5 mg/mL).

questions.q: Polydioxanone (PDO) thread lifts achieve facial rejuvenation by which dual mechanism?
opts: Permanent mechanical lift via barbed sutures anchored to deep fascia with indefinite duration
Immediate tissue repositioning by barbed threads + delayed biostimulation as PDO degrades over 6–9 months, stimulating fibroblast collagen and elastin deposition along the thread tract
Scar tissue bands forming along thread trajectories that permanently anchor ptotic tissue
PDO threads dissolve in 2 weeks, after which only the temporary inflammatory response provides mild lift
questions.exp: PDO threads provide: (1) immediate mechanical effect — barbs/cogs engage dermis and SMAS, repositioning ptotic tissue; (2) delayed biostimulatory effect — PDO hydrolysis over 6–9 months stimulates fibroblasts to deposit type I collagen and elastin along the thread tract. Combined results last 12–18 months. Complications: puckering/dimpling (most common), extrusion, infection, nerve injury. PDO is fully absorbable — no permanent foreign body.

questions.q: In photodynamic therapy (PDT) for actinic keratoses, 5-ALA is applied then activated by light. The primary cytotoxic mediator generated is:
opts: Singlet oxygen (¹O₂) generated from photoactivated protoporphyrin IX (PpIX) reacting with molecular oxygen — causing mitochondrial membrane destruction and apoptosis
Reactive nitrogen species from 5-ALA photoreduction in hypoxic dysplastic cells
Thermally generated hydroxyl radicals from water photolysis at the ALA absorption wavelength
Direct phototoxic 5-ALA metabolite bypassing PpIX accumulation in rapidly proliferating cells
questions.exp: 5-ALA (a haem precursor) is preferentially taken up by hyperproliferative dysplastic cells and converted to photosensitiser PpIX via the haem biosynthesis pathway. Upon activation with red light (630 nm) or blue light (405 nm), PpIX undergoes a Type II photochemical reaction: PpIX + hν + O₂ → singlet oxygen (¹O₂). Singlet oxygen causes lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial damage, and apoptosis of dysplastic cells while sparing lower-PpIX normal cells.

questions.q: Dermabrasion (with diamond fraise or wire brush) differs from microdermabrasion in that dermabrasion:
opts: Only removes the stratum corneum (15 μm) while microdermabrasion reaches the papillary dermis
Penetrates through the full epidermis into the papillary-to-mid reticular dermis, equivalent to a deep peel, treating deep acne scars and rhinophyma
Uses vacuum suction to remove abraded skin debris; microdermabrasion relies on saline irrigation
Is performed under topical anaesthesia and achieves results equivalent to a superficial TCA peel
questions.exp: Dermabrasion reaches papillary-to-mid reticular dermis (depending on speed and pressure), equivalent to a deep chemical peel — appropriate for deep acne scars, rhinophyma, and post-traumatic scars. Re-epithelialization occurs from surviving adnexal structures. Microdermabrasion removes only stratum corneum (15–30 μm), providing superficial exfoliation for mild texture and dyspigmentation only. Dermabrasion requires regional/general anaesthesia and carries significant downtime (7–14 days).

questions.q: During the catagen phase of the hair cycle, the correct sequence of follicular events is:
opts: Melanocytes reactivate to begin pigmenting the incoming anagen shaft
Matrix keratinocyte proliferation ceases, lower follicle involutes, dermal papilla retracts upward forming club hair, secondary germ encapsulates papilla for next anagen
Sebaceous gland hypertrophies transiently to produce protective sebum during follicular transition
Perifollicular lymphocyte infiltration increases, triggering immune-mediated shedding of the telogen hair
questions.exp: Catagen (2–3 weeks): matrix keratinocyte proliferation abruptly stops → lower follicle involutes (⅔ of follicle disappears by apoptosis) → melanocytes lose pigment production → dermal papilla retracts upward → club hair forms (keratinised proximal end held in follicle) → secondary hair germ (follicle epithelial remnant) encapsulates retracted papilla, forming the template for next anagen phase.

questions.q: Permanent hypopigmentation after ablative CO₂ laser resurfacing results from:
opts: Selective photothermolysis of epidermal melanocytes at 10,600 nm wavelength
Thermal destruction of melanocyte progenitor stem cells in the hair follicle bulge region and basal layer, reducing the pool available for epidermal repigmentation
Laser-induced upregulation of TGF-β1 causing permanent tyrosinase suppression in surviving melanocytes
Post-laser fibrosis obliterating follicular structures from which re-epithelialization occurs
questions.exp: Ablative laser resurfacing thermal injury can destroy melanocyte stem cells in the hair follicle bulge and epidermal basal layer — the reservoir for repigmentation after wounding. Loss of this pool prevents melanocyte repopulation, resulting in permanent hypopigmentation, particularly after repeated sessions, very deep passes, or in patients who develop post-laser scarring. This differs from transient PIH which occurs from retained but over-stimulated melanocytes.

questions.q: The 1450 nm diode laser is used for acne treatment. Its target and mechanism of action are:
opts: Melanin in sebaceous duct epithelium — selective follicular destruction via selective photothermolysis
Intracellular water within the sebaceous gland — selective thermal heating reduces gland size and sebum production without surface ablation
Cutibacterium acnes endogenous porphyrins at 1450 nm — photodynamic bactericidal effect
Dermal collagen — post-inflammatory collagen remodelling incidentally reduces post-acne scarring
questions.exp: The 1450 nm diode laser targets water within the sebaceous gland. Glands have high water content relative to surrounding dermis, causing selective thermal injury, reducing gland size and sebum production — removing the substrate for C. acnes colonisation. Cryogen spray protects the epidermis. This is a non-ablative approach requiring 3–5 sessions. Efficacy is comparable to oral isotretinoin for inflammatory acne in some studies.

questions.q: Foam sclerotherapy (e.g., polidocanol foam) is preferred over liquid sclerotherapy for larger varicose veins because:
opts: Foam is less irritating to venous endothelium, reducing post-procedure phlebitis
Foam displaces blood from the vessel lumen, maximising undiluted sclerosant-endothelium contact at lower total sclerosant volumes
Foam is more radiopaque than liquid, allowing fluoroscopic guidance for deep perforator veins
Foam penetrates the vessel wall adventitia, producing a more permanent perivenous fibrosis
questions.exp: Foam sclerotherapy (Tessari method: 1:4 liquid:air or CO₂ ratio) displaces blood from the vessel lumen so undiluted sclerosant contacts the full endothelial surface — producing superior endothelial injury at lower total sclerosant volumes than liquid (which is diluted by blood). Foam is echogenic on duplex ultrasound, enabling real-time guidance for truncal veins. Risks: microembolism, transient visual disturbance (via patent foramen ovale), thrombosis.

questions.q: 1 unit of onabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) is NOT equivalent to 1 unit of abobotulinumtoxinA (Dysport). The correct conversion ratio when switching between products is approximately:
opts: 1:1 — all botulinum toxin type A products are standardised to the same biological activity per unit
1 Botox unit = 2.5–3 Dysport units, due to different mouse LD50 assay methodologies and protein concentrations
1 Botox unit = 10 Dysport units — Dysport is significantly more dilute per unit
1 Botox unit = 0.5 Dysport units — Dysport is twice as potent per unit
questions.exp: Botulinum toxin products are NOT interchangeable unit-for-unit. Allergan's Botox units are defined by their mouse LD50 assay; Ipsen's Dysport uses a different assay method with different protein loading, yielding ~2.5–3 Dysport units = 1 Botox unit for equivalent clinical effect. Xeomin (incobotulinumtoxinA) uses a 1:1 conversion with Botox. Failure to convert when switching products causes significant under- or over-treatment.

questions.q: Repeated low-fluence Q-switched Nd:YAG 1064 nm 'laser toning' for melasma carries a specific long-term risk NOT seen with standard high-fluence single-pass Q-switched laser use. This complication is:
opts: Paradoxical melasma deepening due to MSH stimulation from subthreshold thermal injury
Ink-spot (confetti) leukoderma — permanent macular hypopigmentation from cumulative selective destruction of epidermal melanocytes without triggering melanocyte replacement
Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation from each individual toning session
Permanent textural scarring from repeated subablative dermal microinjury
questions.exp: Low-fluence Q-switched Nd:YAG toning delivers melanin-specific energy insufficient for classical selective photothermolysis but sufficient for cumulative melanocyte injury over multiple sessions. This causes ink-spot leukoderma (confetti hypopigmentation) — permanent white macules from melanocyte destruction without sufficient stimulus for progenitor cell replacement. It is largely irreversible. Recognition of this risk has led to reduced enthusiasm for laser toning protocols exceeding 10 sessions.

questions.q: Retinol, retinaldehyde, and tretinoin differ in potency and irritancy due to their conversion pathway in skin. The correct pathway is:
opts: Retinol → retinoic acid in a single irreversible oxidative step by retinol dehydrogenase
Retinol → retinaldehyde (by retinol dehydrogenases) → all-trans retinoic acid (by retinaldehyde dehydrogenases) — a rate-limited two-step process making retinol ~10–20× less potent than tretinoin
Retinol → retinyl palmitate → retinoic acid, each step requiring UV light activation
Retinol → 9-cis-retinoic acid (binds RXR exclusively); tretinoin → all-trans-retinoic acid (binds RAR exclusively) — entirely different receptor targets
questions.exp: Retinol (vitamin A alcohol) → retinaldehyde (retinal) via retinol dehydrogenases → all-trans-retinoic acid via retinaldehyde dehydrogenases (RALDH). Each conversion step is rate-limited, making retinol ~10–20× less potent and less irritating than topical tretinoin. Retinaldehyde is one conversion step closer — more potent than retinol and better tolerated than tretinoin, making it useful in cosmeceuticals for sensitive skin.

questions.q: When injecting hyaluronidase to reverse an HA filler, which statement about mechanism and dosing is CORRECT?
opts: Hyaluronidase cleaves HA at β-1,3 glycosidic bonds between glucosamine residues
Hyaluronidase cleaves HA at β-1,4 glycosidic bonds; approximately 5–30 IU dissolves ~0.1–0.5 mL of standard HA filler — highly cross-linked products require higher doses
Hyaluronidase also degrades CaHA and PLLA fillers via depolymerisation of their gel matrices
Hyaluronidase activity is inhibited by warmth — avoid warm compresses which reduce enzyme efficacy
questions.exp: Hyaluronidase cleaves β-1,4 glycosidic bonds between N-acetyl-D-glucosamine and D-glucuronate in HA chains. Approximate dosing: 5–30 IU per 0.1–0.5 mL of filler; highly cross-linked products (e.g., Juvederm Voluma) require higher doses than less cross-linked products (e.g., Restylane Silk). Warm compresses increase diffusion of hyaluronidase. It is completely ineffective against non-HA fillers (CaHA, PLLA, silicone, PMMA).

questions.q: SPF (Sun Protection Factor) measures protection against which UV range, and what is the FDA standard for claiming 'broad-spectrum' UVA protection?
opts: SPF measures UVA (320–400 nm) protection; UVB protection is rated by the PPD (persistent pigment darkening) ratio
SPF specifically measures UVB (280–320 nm) erythema protection; FDA broad-spectrum requires critical wavelength ≥370 nm (covering UVA range) on spectrophotometric testing
SPF measures combined UVA + UVB protection on a single scale above SPF 15
SPF measures UVB protection and automatically implies equivalent UVA protection above SPF 50
questions.exp: SPF is defined by the ratio of MED (minimal erythema dose) with vs. without sunscreen, measuring UVB protection only (280–320 nm). UVA (320–400 nm) causes tanning, immunosuppression, photoageing, and melanoma without visible erythema. FDA broad-spectrum claim requires critical wavelength ≥370 nm on in vitro spectrophotometric testing — meaning the product absorbs across the UVA spectrum. PA+/++/++/++++ ratings (Asia/Japan) quantify UVA protection via PPD.

questions.q: Long-term (>6 months) continuous topical hydroquinone use carries a specific serious adverse effect particularly in darker skin types. This is:
opts: Tachyphylaxis — melanocytes upregulate tyrosinase expression, overcoming hydroquinone inhibition and causing treatment failure
Exogenous ochronosis — paradoxical blue-black/slate-grey hyperpigmentation from dermal polymerisation of hydroquinone metabolites, largely irreversible
Systemic toxicity — percutaneous absorption causes nephrotoxicity requiring serum creatinine monitoring
Rebound hyperpigmentation only — permanent adverse pigmentary changes do not occur with topical use
questions.exp: Exogenous ochronosis is a paradoxical blue-black hyperpigmentation in HQ-treated areas, more common in darker skin types (FST IV–VI) with prolonged use. Mechanism: HQ metabolites (benzoquinone acetic acid) polymerise to ochre-coloured deposits that accumulate in the dermis when not fully excreted. Histology shows yellow-brown banana-shaped fibres replacing collagen. It is largely irreversible. Prevention: use HQ in cycles (max 8–12 weeks), stop if pigmentation worsens.

questions.q: Microneedling for striae distensae (stretch marks) — the correct needle depth and mechanism of improvement are:
opts: 0.25 mm — targets epidermis, improving striae surface texture by increasing epidermal thickness
1.5–2.5 mm — reaches the atrophic dermal zone, stimulating fibroblast-mediated type I/III collagen and elastin synthesis
3.0–3.5 mm — targets subcutaneous fat, stimulating adipogenesis to restore volume in deep striae distensae
0.5–1.0 mm — papillary dermis stimulation is adequate for striae distensae alba (white striae)
questions.exp: Striae distensae involve mid-to-deep dermal atrophy with disrupted collagen and elastin fibres. Microneedling at 1.5–2.5 mm targets this atrophic zone, stimulating fibroblast activation via TGF-β and PDGF signalling to synthesise new type I and III collagen and elastin. Open channels also allow delivery of topical growth factors or PRP. Striae rubrae (active, pink) respond better than alba (mature, white). Typically 3–6 sessions required at 4–6 week intervals.

questions.q: Mesotherapy for androgenetic alopecia (AGA) involves mid-dermal microinjections. The most evidence-supported active component in mesotherapy cocktails is:
opts: Finasteride 0.1% for direct local DHT inhibition within the follicular unit
Minoxidil (0.5–1%) combined with biotin and peptide mixtures — improving local scalp vascularity and follicular microenvironment
Platelet-poor plasma (PPP) providing baseline growth factor concentrations to the dermal papilla
Corticosteroids reducing perifollicular inflammation that causes miniaturisation in AGA
questions.exp: Mesotherapy protocols are heterogeneous, but combinations of minoxidil (anagen-prolonging K+ channel opener) + biotin (keratin synthesis cofactor) + peptide mixtures (growth signal mimetics, e.g., copper peptides, biotinoyl tripeptide-1) have the most clinical evidence for AGA. Intradermal minoxidil bypasses the SULT1A1 conversion bottleneck and delivers higher follicular concentrations than topical diffusion. Evidence quality remains limited by absence of standardised RCT protocols.

questions.q: The Jessner's solution + TCA 35% combination peel for melasma in Fitzpatrick skin type III. The role of Jessner's solution pre-treatment is:
opts: To achieve a more superficial peel by buffering TCA penetration with its acidic components
To degrease and create uniform superficial epidermolysis, allowing more homogeneous and deeper TCA penetration at a lower (safer) TCA concentration than would otherwise be required
To provide antifungal prophylaxis for the post-peel period of skin barrier disruption
To stimulate Langerhans cell migration to the epidermis, priming the immune system for melanocyte suppression
questions.exp: Jessner's solution (resorcinol 14% + salicylic acid 14% + lactic acid 14% in ethanol) acts as a 'primer': it degreases skin and creates a controlled superficial epidermolysis, allowing TCA 35% to penetrate uniformly and more deeply than it would on intact skin — achieving consistent papillary dermal depth without needing higher (riskier) TCA concentrations. This combination is a classic medium-depth peel. Risk of PIH is increased in FST III+ patients requiring careful post-peel sun protection.
